issues.item: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance and safety-positioning in response to interpersonal danger, but no other item suggests contamination, orderliness, or a ritualised control theme. As a maladaptive strategy, it feels disconnected from the threat pattern represented here.

issues.item: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
issues.explanation: The formulation has Threat strongly linked with Maladaptive Strategies, while Memory is isolated with no active edges. The maladaptive strategy items should therefore be tightly connected to current threat management. 'Memory Detachment' is a memory-focused coping response that implies an active Memory-related process, which is not reflected elsewhere and does not align with the specified edge pattern. In contrast, reassurance seeking, hypervigilance towards people, and the threat items form a coherent threat-management cluster for captivity trauma.

vignette: John is a 53-year-old male of Oceania ethnicity who has been married for over three decades. He works as a photographer and his life took a dramatic turn several months ago when he was held captive by kidnappers for nearly two weeks. Since then, John's daily life has become increasingly difficult to navigate due to the persistent presence of PTSD symptoms. During the captivity, John felt utterly powerless and constantly watched over by his captors. This experience left him with an enduring sense that danger lurks around every corner. Now, he is hyper-aware of sudden movements made by others, which immediately puts him on high alert. He feels a constant tension in his body, as if it's always primed to react to any threat. John’s heightened state of vigilance has led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies that he uses to cope with his ongoing fear and anxiety. For instance, before entering any location, whether it is for work or leisure, he meticulously plans an escape route. He feels more secure if he knows exactly how to leave quickly in case danger arises. This constant planning consumes much of his mental energy and often overshadows the actual task at hand. Furthermore, John always selects seating arrangements based on how safe and protected they feel. When dining out or attending social gatherings, he will choose a seat that allows him a clear view of all entrances and exits. He believes that sitting in such positions reduces his vulnerability to sudden attacks. This behavior is deeply rooted in the belief that by positioning himself strategically, he can better protect himself from potential threats. John’s hypervigilance has also led him to seek constant reassurance from those around him. He frequently asks his wife and colleagues if they think he is okay or if there are any signs of danger nearby. This need for validation and assurance stems directly from his heightened sense of threat. Despite receiving repeated assurances, John often finds himself doubting these words and feeling even more anxious. The cycle between threat perception and maladaptive strategies has become self-reinforcing in John’s life. His constant body tension and hypervigilance towards sudden movements by others have led him to seek reassurance frequently, which only serves to heighten his sense of vulnerability further. Each time he receives reassurance but still feels threatened, it reinforces the belief that he must remain vigilant at all times. John's occupation as a photographer has been particularly impacted by these symptoms. He often avoids photo shoots in crowded places, fearing that the sudden movements of people might trigger an overwhelming response from his body. This avoidance has led to missed opportunities and strained working relationships with clients who do not understand his reluctance to work in certain environments. Despite his efforts to manage his symptoms through maladaptive strategies, John finds himself increasingly isolated and anxious. His wife notices that he is more distant and less engaged in their shared activities. He also feels a growing sense of frustration at the limitations these symptoms have imposed on his life. What finally brought John to seek help was a recent incident where he almost missed an important family event due to his fears about entering crowded spaces. This realization made him acutely aware that he needed support to break this cycle and regain control over his life. John is most hoping for strategies that will allow him to feel safe again and reduce the constant tension in his body, so he can return to enjoying both his work and family time without fear. In conclusion, John's experience of captivity has left a profound mark on his daily functioning, manifesting through persistent hypervigilance and maladaptive coping mechanisms. His journey towards recovery is just beginning, but with the right support, he hopes to regain a sense of safety and peace in his life.
